ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the circuit is a 120 V DC power supply; above there is a single-pole double-throw switch S, which can connect to point 1 or point 2. Point 1 is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply; the common terminal of the switch is connected through the upper 20 Ω resistor to the coil branch on the right side. The coil branch on the right side is composed of an inductor labeled 10 H and a 40 Ω resistor connected in series, with the bottom end connected to the common lower conductor. Point 2 is connected downward to an unknown resistor R, and then connected to the bottom common node. Reasoning: After switch S contacts point 1 for a very long time, the circuit reaches DC steady state, and the 10 H inductor is equivalent to a short circuit. At this time, what is in series in the power supply loop is the 20 Ω resistor and the coil internal resistance 40 Ω, so the steady-state current is I0 = 120 / (20 + 40) = 2 A. The inductor current cannot change abruptly, so at t = 0+, the inductor current is still 2 A, in the same direction as before switching. After the switch is switched to point 2, this 2 A current passes through the closed loop composed of R, the 20 Ω resistor, and the coil branch. According to the specified method, at t = 0+, the magnitude of the voltage across the two ends of the coil is equal to the voltage drop on the external path R + 20 Ω, so 120 = 2(R + 20). Solving gives R + 20 = 60, therefore R = 40 Ω.

raw_record.question_text: A coil of inductance 10 H and resistance 40 \(\Omega\) is connected as shown in the figure. After the switch \(S\) has been in contact with point 1 for a very long time, it is moved to point 2 at \(t = 0\). method.method_draft: First, with S at point 1 for a long time, replace the inductor by a short. The current through the 20 Ω resistor and the coil resistance 40 Ω is I0 = 120/(20+40) = 2 A. At t = 0+, the inductor current is still 2 A in the same direction. After the switch moves to point 2, this current circulates through R, the 20 Ω resistor, and the coil branch. The terminal voltage across the coil assembly equals the drop across the external path R + 20 Ω, so 120 = 2(R+20). Solve for R = 40 Ω.
